Learning Objectives
Describe imaging studies for evaluation of the knee.

Overview

Overview
The goal of this lesson is to review imaging studies frequently used in the evaluation of
knee injury and pathology. Imaging studies are an important adjunct to the patient
history and physical examination, enabling a complete assessment of a patient’s

condition. Appropriate imaging studies allows for efficient and accurate diagnosis and
uses resources in a cost-effective manner.
Types of imaging studies
Plain radiography
CT
MRI
Ultrasonography
Nuclear medicine
Positron emission tomography (PET)
Bone scintigraphy
Radiographs help confirm the clinical diagnosis of a joint disorder that has been
determined via the patient history and physical examination findings. Plain radiographs
are appropriate initial imaging studies for most knee conditions because they allow for
assessment of traumatic injury, arthritis, alignment, osteochondral injury, bone
neoplasm, and prior surgical implants. Advanced imaging studies may be indicated to
assess bony detail and anatomy (CT) and to evaluate intra-articular and extra-articular
soft-tissue structures, such as cartilage, menisci, ligaments, tendons, muscles, and nerve
and vascular structures (MRI). Ultrasonography may be useful in the assessment of more
superficial knee pathology, including issues with the extensor mechanism and other
extra-articular structures. Nuclear medicine studies, including bone scans and other
specialized imaging studies, may provide additional information in specific clinical
situations. Resource 1

Overview
Imaging studies should include at least two perpendicular views: AP and lateral.
Pathology that is visible in only one plane may be missed on single-view images, limiting
assessment of joint alignment.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:26 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002092
7/39

Weight-bearing views of the knee provide a more sensitive assessment of joint space
narrowing from degenerative conditions by compressing the joint space.1 AP extension
views are useful for assessment of any joint space loss on the extension surface; flexed-
knee views are more useful for assessment of cartilage loss on the flexion surfaces
(damage of the flexion surface often precedes damage on the extension surface of the
femur, particularly on the lateral side).2
Lateral radiographs are particularly useful for evaluation of the patella and the extensor
mechanism and provide an orthogonal view of the femur from the anteroposterior. The
clinician can assess the height of the patella and the presence of trochlear dysplasia (risk
factor for patellar instability) and evaluate patellar fractures for displacement.
Patellofemoral, or axial knee, views are obtained to assess patellar subluxation and
degenerative change in the patellofemoral joint. A Merchant view typically is obtained
from proximal to distal with the knee in lower degrees of flexion (approximately 30°).3
This view is used to assess patellar subluxation before the patella centers into the
trochlear groove in deeper knee flexion. A sunrise view in obtained in a distal-to-
proximal direction with the knee in deeper flexion (>90°).4 This view is most useful for
evaluation of patellofemoral joint degenerative changes and joint space loss because the
high knee flexion angle does not allow for accurate assessment of patellar subluxation
that typically occurs at lower flexion angles.
Full-length lower extremity views can be obtained to assess lower extremity alignment
(varus/valgus at the knee) and to identify leg-length differences.
Clinical Indications
Trauma
Fracture of the distal femur, proximal tibia, patella, or tibial tuberosity
A bipartite patella involves an unfused ossification center, commonly at the superolateral
patella (Figure 6).
Dislocation of the tibiofemoral or patellofemoral joint
Injury of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)/Segond fracture (Figure 7)

Injury of the medial collateral ligament (MCL)
Knee pain
Osteoarthritis—Radiography may identify subchondral sclerosis, joint space narrowing,
subchondral cysts (variable), osteophytes (variable), and joint subluxation (Figure 8).
Inflammatory arthropathy: joint space loss, peripheral bone erosion
Osteochondral defects: subchondral radiolucency, most common in the medial femoral
condyle
Stress fracture: linear radiolucency or radiodensity, most common in the proximal medial
tibia
Osteonecrosis: mixed sclerotic pattern with a subchondral, epiphyseal, or metaphyseal
location; may be a stable lesion or associated with collapse
Patellofemoral disease: malalignment, osteophytes, cysts, joint space loss

Clinical Indications
In the absence of acute trauma, plain weight-bearing radiographs generally are obtained
to assess for degenerative changes. A lateral radiograph also aids in identification of an
effusion that would indicate intra-articular pathology.
Non–weight-bearing radiographs may identify acute injury without the risk of fracture
displacement. Typically, orthogonal (AP and lateral) views are obtained along with 45°
oblique views to increase sensitivity for detection of fractures.
Bipartite patellae commonly are confused with fractures, and they can be symptomatic,
particularly after trauma. Increased signal on T2-weighted MRI suggests movement at

Lateral capsule (anterolateral ligament) avulsion (Segond fracture) is pathognomonic but
not essential for ACL injury.5,6 Hemarthrosis frequently is identified as an effusion on the
lateral radiograph.
Avulsion of the medial femoral epicondyle is very rare. Ossification at the MCL origin
(Pellegrini-Stieda lesion) may appear after a proximal MCL injury7 (Figure 11).
In the absence of acute trauma, plain weight-bearing radiographs generally are obtained
to assess for degenerative changes. A lateral radiograph also aids in identification of an
effusion that would indicate intra-articular pathology.

Clinical indications
Periarticular fractures
Assessment of joint arthroplasty implants for loosening
Osteolytic lesions around implants can be assessed via CT as an adjunct to plain
radiographs.
Infection and neoplasia
CT allows for detailed assessment of cortical disruption in cases patients with infection or
neoplasia.
Preoperative planning
Assessment of limb rotational alignment
Intra-articular pathology in patients who cannot undergo MRI


Computed Tomography
Imaging in the axial, sagittal, and coronal planes along with three-dimensional
reconstruction images improve identification and assessment of fracture lines and
displacement compared with plain radiographs.
CT, particularly with three-dimensional reconstruction images, may aid in preoperative
planning for complex intra-articular fractures (Figure 13), multiplanar osteotomy for
limb malalignment, management of patellar instability, and revision ligament
reconstruction procedures in which prior bone tunnels may affect surgical technique
(Figure 14). They also aid in assessment of bone loss in planning for total joint
arthroplasty.
Axial imaging of the hip and knee may aid in assessment of the rotational alignment of
the patellofemoral joint of the native knee or of components of a total knee arthroplasty
implant in patients with patellar maltracking.
Some patients in whom intra-articular pathology is suspected have implanted devices
(such as internal defibrillators) that preclude the use of MRI. In these patients, CT
arthrography can allow for assessment for injury to the ACL, posterior cruciate ligament
(PCL), menisci, and articular cartilage.8 Although inferior to MRI, CT arthrography may be
a useful tool in this patient population.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
General information
MRI allows for assessment of soft-tissue anatomy and bone.
Increasing strength of the magnetic field (measured in Tesla units) increases the resolution of
images.
An injected contrast agent (intravenous or intra-articular) may help delineate specific tissues
of interest in specific patients.
Clinical indications
Cruciate ligament injury (ACL/PCL)
Meniscal injury
Articular cartilage

Extra-articular ligaments
Tendon injury
Neurovascular structures

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Edema, intra-articular fluid, disruption of ligament fibers, and an atypical ligament
contour suggest injury. T2-weighted MRIs are most useful for identification of acute
ligament injuries (Figure 15), whereas the better anatomic resolution of T1-weighted
MRIs may allow for assessment of chronic ACL tears via direct visualization of the
ligament (Figure 16). A key MRI finding suggestive of acute ACL injury is bone bruises,
primarily in the lateral compartment. Best visualized on T2-weighted sagittal MRIs, the
bruises typically are located in the central one-third of the lateral femoral condyle and
the posterior one-third of the lateral tibial plateau (Figure 17). Recent studies also have
demonstrated that injuries to the anterolateral ligament complex can be identified on
MRI after ACL injury.9

MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for the evaluation of meniscal pathology.
Patterns of meniscal injury can be identified by location (anterior, midbody, posterior,
peripheral, central, root [Figures 18 and 19]), pattern (horizontal [Figure 20],
longitudinal [Figure 21], radial, complex), and displacement (including bucket-handle
tears [Figure 22]). Bucket-handle tears of the medial meniscus can be identified via the
double PCL sign on sagittal MRIs (Figure 23). Intra-articular contrast may be a useful
adjunct to evaluate meniscal tears for healing after repair.10 Even with MRI
arthrography, identification of recurrent tears in patients who have undergone prior
meniscal surgery may be difficult.

location (medial condyle, lateral condyle, trochlea, patella) and aspect (anterior,

MRI may be used to assess the margin of resection for a neoplasm, identify vascular
malformation, or define the location of nerves or vessels relative to popliteal cysts.
Ultrasonography
General information
Ultrasonography is an emerging technique for imaging in the musculoskeletal system, with
additional indications being described.
Ultrasonography is limited in the depth of tissue that can be evaluated and by the experience
of the individual performing the procedure.
Clinical indications
Extensor mechanism
Other indications

9/3/26, 4:26 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002092


Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography can be used to identify tears of the quadriceps or patellar tendon;
however, more frequently, it is used to evaluate for the presence and severity of
tendinosis of these tendons. Ultrasonographic guidance can be used for peritendinous
injections and other percutaneous therapies.
Ultrasonography can be used to detect meniscal tears; however, its sensitivity is poorer
than that of MRI.11 A potential advantage of ultrasonography for meniscus evaluation is
the ability to assess meniscal extrusion dynamically and as the patient is bearing weight.
Although ultrasonography is not a good imaging modality for evaluation of the cruciate
ligaments, it may allow for visualization of secondary injuries to the anterolateral
complex, including avulsion injuries (Segond fractures).12
Nuclear Medicine Studies
Positron Emission Tomography
General information
PET is a functional imaging modality that can be used to assess metabolic activity. These
imaging studies are obtained via labeled radionuclide injection followed by delayed imaging
of gamma radiation.
Areas of increased radionuclide concentration appear bright or hot.
It provides a nonspecific study that does not define the etiology of an abnormality but rather
the presence of an abnormality that may correlate with a clinical concern.
It involves the use of various radioactive tracers, including fluorodeoxyglucose and sodium
fluoride , gallium 67and indium 111.
PET scans can be superimposed on CT scans or MRIs to provide greater anatomic resolution
than that of bone scans at lower radiation doses.
Clinical indications

9/3/26, 4:26 PM


Positron Emission Tomography
Clinical indications for PET in the knee are limited; however, early studies demonstrate
some utility of PET-MRI to assess graft ligamentization after ACL reconstruction.13
Gallium-67 may help differentiate aseptic prosthetic loosening from septic prosthetic
loosening; 24 to 72 hours are necessary for a complete study. Indium 111 is used in
leukocyte scanning, in which white blood cells are labeled and assessed. Indium 111 is
more likely to concentrate in areas of acute infection and frequently is used in patients
with spine infection, among others.14
Bone Scintigraphy
General information
Bone scans are nuclear medicine studies that typically involve the use of technetium-99m or
other radionuclides to assess bone metabolic activity.
Uptake is assessed with the use of a gamma camera.
Clinical indications

Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scans can be used to identify musculoskeletal infection, neoplasia, or occult
fracture, as well as to assess bone healing, phases of heterotopic ossification, implant
loosening, or failure of osseointegration.15
Increased radionuclide activity in bone may be a normal postoperative finding for as
long as 6 to 12 months after fracture repair or arthroplasty.
